summary: This record covers the dynamic and four-dimensional splat research beyond the base technique row: the reference implementations that reconstruct a moving scene, the 2026 work on compressing and streaming one, and the commercial service that sells the result as volumetric video. The methods disagree about where time lives. Shape of Motion reconstructs a moving scene from a single ordinary video by learning a small set of shared motion bases; 4D-Rotor Gaussians make the primitive itself four-dimensional with a rotor-based rotation; MoSca fits a deformable scaffold to casual video; and the newest work treats a moving scene as a bitstream to be pruned, quantised and layered. All of it is research code with a research licence or none at all, most of it needs CUDA, and none of it writes a format any other implementation reads. The 2026 streaming papers state the interoperability problem in the plainest words this map has found anywhere: a four-dimensional model is a monolithic bitstream that a client must download in full before a single frame can be drawn, with first-frame waits measured in tens to hundreds of seconds on a mobile link. The one production pipeline in the family, Gracia, sells processed volumetric video delivered through its own engine kits and ships either a proprietary container or a numbered sequence of PLY files — which is exactly the flipbook the base technique row already describes, five hundred papers later.

coverage.note: Every member of the family carries its own rasteriser, usually a modified copy of one reference implementation with a time term added, and none describes a pass structure. The four-dimensional rotor work is unusual in making the primitive itself four-dimensional rather than deforming a three-dimensional one.
